label: theorem:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theorem:main}
For $g = 2$ and any $n$, we have $H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,n}) = S^{15}_\omega(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,n})$.

title: Remark

As noted in the survey article \cite[Proposition 3.9]{Lsurvey}, the cases
$(g,n) = (3,9), (4,7), (5,5), (6,3),$ and $(7,1)$ follow readily from results already in the literature. The proofs for the other cases above utilize our new results on $S_\omega^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$.

label: lemma:topweight
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:topweight} If $g \geq 2$, $n \geq k$ and $n >0$ then
\[
W_kH^k(\mathcal M_{g,n}) = \pi_1^*W_kH^k(\mathcal M_{g,n-1}) + \cdots + \pi_n^*W_kH^k(\mathcal M_{g,n-1})\, ,
\]
where $\pi_i \colon \mathcal M_{g,n} \to \mathcal M_{g,n-1}$ is the tautological morphism forgetting the $i$th marking.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In fact, the other cases when $g = 2$ and $n \leq 13$ already follow from results in the literature.
When $n \leq 10$, we have $\dim \overline{\mathcal M}_{2,n} \leq 13$ and so $H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,n})$ is Poincar\'e dual to $H^{k}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,n})$ for some odd $k \leq 11$. Thus, $H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,n}) = 0$ for $n \leq 10$.
For $n = 11$, \cite[Lemma 3.2]{CLP24extensions} then implies that $H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,11}) = S^{15}_\omega(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,11})$.
Next,
\cite[Lemma 7.3]{CLP24extensions} states that $H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,12}) = S^{15}_\omega(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,12})$.
Hence, another application of \cite[Lemma 3.2]{CLP24extensions}  implies $H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,13}) = S^{15}_\omega(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,13})$.
head: environment

label: 132reduction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{132reduction}
Fix some $g \geq 2$ and any $n$. 
We have $H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) = S_\omega^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$ if and only if
$H^{13,2}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) = S_\omega^{13,2}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have $H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) = S_\omega^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$ if and only if $H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) \otimes \mathbb{C} = S^{15}_\omega(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) \otimes \mathbb{C}$. Since $g \geq 2$, \cite[Theorem 1.1]{CLP24extensions} tells us that $H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) \otimes \mathbb{C} = H^{13,2}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) \oplus H^{2,13}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$. Meanwhile, the decorated graph generators for $S^{15}_\omega(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) \otimes \mathbb{C}$ involve only decorations of type $(11,0), (0,11), (1,1)$, so
$S^{15}_\omega(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})\otimes \mathbb{C} = S^{13,2}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) \oplus S^{2,13}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$. Thus, we have  $H^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) = S_\omega^{15}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$ if and only if $H^{13,2}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) = S_\omega^{13,2}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$.
head: environment

label: lem:span
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:span}
Without imposing the restrictions in the third column, the classes displayed in Figure \ref{fig:gentable} generate $S^{13,2}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A decorated graph generator for $S^{13,2}_\omega(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$ can have one or two edges. We consider classes of each type in turn.

First suppose that the graph has two edges. In this case, the only decoration is an $\omega$-decoration on a genus-$1$ vertex. Possibilities for this decorated graph are given in the first five rows in Figure \ref{fig:gentable}. We now explain why only the listed $\omega$-decorations are necessary.
For classes of type $\mathcal S$ or type $\mathcal L$,
only the decorations $\omega_{B \cup p}$ are needed because they form a basis for $H^{11,0}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{1, (X \cup Y)^c \cup p})$ by \cite[Corollary 2.4]{CLP23eleventh}. For classes of type $\mathcal M$ and $\mathcal N$ (which have the same underlying graph), consider $H^{11,0}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,(X \cup Y)^c \cup \{p, q\}})$ together with the $S_2$ action that exchanges $p$ and $q$. The $S_2$-invariant subspace is spanned by the decorations $\omega_B^{S_2}$ for $B \subset (X \cup Y)^c$ with $|B| = 10$. Meanwhile, the
$S_2$ anti-invariant subspace is spanned by the classes $\omega_{B' \cup p \cup q}$ for $B' \subset (X \cup Y)^c$ with $|B'| = 9$. Thus, the listed $\omega$-decorated graphs span all $\omega$-decorated graphs of this type.
Finally, the graph for classes of type $\mathcal D$ has an automorphism exchanging the two edges which acts on the genus-$1$ vertex by exchanging $p$ and $q$. Since the pushforward along gluing equals the composition of the automorphism with the gluing map, all $S_2$ anti-invariant decorations would yield $0$.



Now suppose that the graph has one edge. If the edge is a self-edge, then the unique vertex in the graph would have genus $g-1$ and require a decoration in $H^{13}$ to produce a class in $H^{15}$. Replacing the class in $H^{13}$ with the corresponding $\omega$-decorated graph would yield a two-edged decorated graph.
Therefore, we may assume that the graph has two vertices: one vertex is genus-$1$ with an $\omega$-decoration, while the other vertex has a decoration in $H^2 = H^{1,1}$. If the decoration in $H^2$ is a boundary divisor, then again, we can expand the graph to have two edges. Thus, it suffices to assume the $H^2$ decoration is a $\psi$ or $\kappa$ class.
Meanwhile, by \cite[Corollary 2.4]{CLP23eleventh}, the $\omega$ decorations $\omega_{B \cup p} \in H^{11,0}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{X^c \cup \{p\}})$ form a basis. Thus, the last two rows in the chart in Figure \ref{fig:gentable} cover all of the needed $1$-edged generators.

label: lem:rel11
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have that $H^{13,2}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,11})$ is Poincar\'e dual to $H^{1,12}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,11})$. A basis for $H^{1,12}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,11})$ is given by the (conjugate) $Z_{B \subset A}$ classes for $B \subset A \subset [11]$, defined in \cite[Section 4]{CLPW24polynomial}. There are $11$ choices for the set $B$ of size $10$ and then either $A = B$ or $A = [11]$. Hence $\dim H^{13,2}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,11}) = 22$. 
After taking into account (R1) -- (R6) and (R9) and (R10), there are $33$ generators remaining, namely
$\mathcal D_{[11] \smallsetminus i, i}$, $\mathcal L_{[11] \smallsetminus i, i}$, and $\mathcal S^0_{[11] \smallsetminus i, i, \varnothing}$, each for $i \in [11]$. Thus, there must be an $11$-dimensional space of relations among these classes.

One readily checks that the class given in the statement of the lemma pairs to zero with each of the conjugate $Z_{B \subset A}$, hence defines a relation. 
Since this gives $11$ relations and $\dim H^{13,2}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,11}) = 22$, 
there can be no other relations.
head: environment

label: rel12
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
To explain the signs, recall that an $\omega$-decoration $\omega_A$ is anti-symmetric in the order of the size $11$ subset $A$. 
If we apply the automorphism that swaps $j$ and $k$, then we will be inserting $j$ into the position of $k$ in some set $A$, which may make it no longer increasing. This is why there are additional signs in the statement of these relations. In the case that $k = j+1$, this swap does not require reordering and the formula for $M_{jk}$ is easily seen to be symmetric in $j$ and $k$.

title: Definition
body_md:
~\cite[Definition~4.1]{CLP24extensions}
    Let $X$ be a smooth algebraic stack of finite type over a field, stratified by quotient stacks. We say that $X$ has the \textit{Chow--Künneth generation Property} (CKgP) if for all algebraic stacks $Y$ (of finite type, stratified by quotient stacks) the exterior product
    \[
    A_*(X) \otimes A_*(Y) \to A_*(X \times Y)
    \]
    is surjective, where $A_*(X)$ and $A_*(Y)$ are the Chow groups of $X$ and $Y$ respectively.

label: lem: implies taut for many g,n
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: implies taut for many g,n}
Suppose $H^*(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) = RH^*(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$ for $(g,n) = (3,9), (4,8)$ and $(5,7)$. Then $H^*(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}) = RH^*(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$ for all $(g,n)$ in Theorem \ref{thm:rh}.
head: environment
labels: lem: implies taut for many g,n

title: Proof
body_md:
In \cite[$\mathsection$5]{Lsurvey}, it is shown that the fact that the cohomology of $\overline{\mathcal M}_{3,9}$ is tautological implies that the cohomology of $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}$ is tautological for $(g,n)\in \{(4,7), (5,5), (6,3), (7,1)\}$. We will review this argument supposing the cohomology of $\overline{\mathcal M}_{4,8}$ is tautological, and show this implies that the cohomology of $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}$ is tautological for $(g,n) \in \{(5,6),(6,4),(7,2),(8,0)\}$.
  
 To prove the case $(g,n) = (5,6)$, we consider the exact sequence
    \[
    H^{k-2}( \widetilde{\partial\mathcal M_{5,6}}) \to H^k(\overline{\mathcal M}_{5,6}) \to W_kH^k(\mathcal M_{5,6}).
    \]
By Table \ref{tab:c-values}, $W_kH^k(\mathcal M_{5,6})$ is generated by tautological classes. Thus, it suffices to prove that all classes pushed forward from the boundary are also tautological. We assume $\overline{\mathcal M}_{4,8}$ is tautological and so all classes from the irreducible boundary divisor are also tautological. Now consider a separating boundary divisor which is the image of a gluing map
    \[
    \overline{\mathcal M}_{g_1,n_1+1} \times \overline{\mathcal M}_{g_2, n_2+1} \to \overline{\mathcal M}_{5,6}.
    \]
   By the smaller cases of Theorem \ref{thm:rh} already established, every $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g_i,n_i+1}$ appearing as a factor of a separating boundary divisor has tautological cohomology. The proofs for the remaining pairs of $(g,n)\in \{(6,4),(7,2),(8,0)\}$ are similar. 

    The remaining $(g,n)$ in Theorem \ref{thm:rh} are proved by the same argument applied to $\overline{\mathcal M}_{5,7}$.

label: lem:S2-invariants-H11
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:S2-invariants-H11}
Let $11 \leq n \leq 20$ and $2m \leq n$, and let $\mathbb{S}_2^{m} \subset \mathbb{S}_n$ be the Young subgroup generated by $m$ disjoint transpositions. If $m \geq n-10$ then the invariant subspace $H^{11}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,n})^{\mathbb{S}_2^m}=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Proposition~2.3]{CLP23eleventh}, the $\mathbb S_n$-representation underlying each Hodge summand of $H^{11}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,n})$ is the hook representation
$$
V_{(n-10,1^{10})}
\cong
\bigwedge^{10}\mathrm{Std}_n,
$$
where $\mathrm{Std}_n$ denotes the standard representation of $\mathbb S_n$. Restricting the standard representation to $\mathbb{S}_2^m$ gives
$$
\operatorname{Res}^{\mathbb S_n}_{\mathbb{S}_2^m}\mathrm{Std}_n
\cong
\mathbf{1}^{\oplus(n-m-1)}
\oplus
\chi_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_m,
$$
where $\chi_i$ is the nontrivial character of the $i$th factor of $\mathbb{S}_2^m$. Since the characters $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_m$ are independent, the product of any nonempty subset of them is nontrivial. Therefore,
$$
\left(\bigwedge^{10}\mathrm{Std}_n\right)^{\mathbb{S}_2^m}
\cong
\bigwedge^{10}\mathbf{1}^{\oplus(n-m-1)}.
$$
If $m\geq n-10$, then $n-m-1\leq 9$, so the right-hand side vanishes.
head: environment

label: cor:graph-averaging-vanishing
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:graph-averaging-vanishing}
Let $\Gamma$ be a stable graph with a genus-one vertex $v$ incident to $n$ half edges. Suppose that a decoration of $\Gamma$ has the form
$$
\gamma=\alpha\otimes\beta,
\qquad
\alpha\in H^{11}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,n}),
$$
where $\beta\in \bigotimes_{w \in V(\Gamma) \smallsetminus \{v\}} H^{k(w)}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g(w),n(w)} )$ denotes the decorations on all remaining vertices. Assume that $\operatorname{Aut}(\Gamma)$ contains a subgroup
$
K \cong \mathbb{S}_2^m
$
that fixes $v$ and $\beta$, and acts on the half edges incident to $v$ by $m$ disjoint transpositions. If $11 \leq n \leq 20$ and $m\geq n-10$, then the associated decorated graph vanishes upon pushforward along the gluing morphism $\xi_\Gamma$.
